central_question: Why does your phone sometimes feel like it vibrated when it didn't?
hook: You’re reaching for your phone, fingers trembling, only to find the screen still dark. It’s not a glitch—your brain is tricking you.
aha_moment: The brain’s predictive model of a phone’s buzz turns any faint tactile cue into a phantom vibration.

story_arc.reveal: A hand reaches for a phone that hasn’t buzzed.
required_facts: People report phantom vibrations 80% of the time in studies
The sensation feels identical to a real buzz

story_arc.reveal: Phantom Vibration Syndrome (PVS) is a real, widespread illusion.
required_facts: PVS coined in 2012 study by Drouin et al.
It’s not a hallucination but a tactile illusion

story_arc.reveal: Your brain builds a forward model that expects a buzz whenever the phone is near.
required_facts: Predictive sensorimotor attenuation uses an efference copy
The model is strengthened by daily phone use

story_arc.reveal: The brain’s copy of the motor command signals the somatosensory cortex to expect vibration, lowering the threshold for ‘yes’ responses.
required_facts: Efference copy suppresses real input but biases perception
Studies by Voss & Haggard (2006) demonstrate this effect

story_arc.reveal: Expectation shifts the decision criterion in signal‑detection theory—any ambiguous touch is labeled a buzz.
required_facts: Signal‑detection theory predicts higher false alarms under expectation
Kilteni & Ehrsson (2022) showed this bias in tactile tasks

story_arc.reveal: Muscle twitches, clothing shifts, or low‑frequency floor vibrations become the seed for the illusion when primed.
required_facts: Peripheral sensory noise is omnipresent
Even a slight fabric tug can feel like a buzz when expecting one

story_arc.reveal: Months of phone‑carrying reshapes hand somatosensory maps, making the brain even more sensitive to vibration‑like cues.
required_facts: Deb (2014) found cortical reorganization after long‑term phone use
Somatosensory maps adapt to frequent stimuli

story_arc.reveal: Even with the phone turned off or in airplane mode, phantom vibrations persist—there’s no mechanical source.
required_facts: Rothberg (2010) recorded phantom buzzes with phones off
NPR (2019) confirmed the effect in Faraday cages

story_arc.reveal: People with higher attachment anxiety report more phantom vibrations, showing a link to emotional expectancies.
required_facts: Attachment anxiety correlates with PVS frequency
Psychological factors modulate sensory predictions

story_arc.reveal: Prediction + attention + noise + plasticity = a false‑alarm in tactile perception.
required_facts: Combined model explains 80% of reported phantom buzzes
It’s a normal by‑product of our predictive brain

ending_payoff: Next time your hand jerks at an empty pocket, remember: you’re just your brain’s way of keeping the phone’s buzz alive—even when the phone is silent.
